title: 2026 CAP/ADASP Guideline: Interpretive Diagnostic Error Reduction in Surgical Pathology and Cytology
journal: College of American Pathologists with the Association of Directors of Anatomic and Surgical Pathology
breakthrough: CAP and ADASP convened an expert interdisciplinary panel to update the 2016 Interpretive Diagnostic Error Reduction guideline, asking what the most effective ways are to reduce interpretive diagnostic error in anatomic pathology, and reviewing new evidence, changed practice environments and the adoption of digital tools. The update issues two strong recommendations supported by moderate-certainty evidence: pathologists should establish formal procedures for reviewing cases to identify diagnostic disagreements and potential interpretive errors, and those reviews should be completed quickly enough to influence patient management.
impact: Puts the emphasis on timeliness as much as on the existence of review. A discrepancy found after the patient has started treatment is a quality statistic; the same discrepancy found before is a corrected diagnosis.
practical: Audit your own department against the second recommendation, which is the one usually failed: review that happens, but too late to change anything. Interpretive diagnostic error means the interpretation of tissue, cytopathology or autopsy material failing to produce a prompt accurate diagnosis, and the consequences named are treatment delay and inappropriate therapy. Note the strength: two strong recommendations on moderate-certainty evidence, not a large prescriptive framework.
link: CAP — Interpretive Diagnostic Error Reduction guideline

verify.status: corrected — real guideline, the specific requirements described are not in it
verify.note: The guideline is real, jointly sponsored by CAP and ADASP, and is a 2026 update of the 2016 'Interpretive Diagnostic Error Reduction in Surgical Pathology and Cytology' guideline. CORRECTION TO CONTENT. The submission says it 'Formally requires pathology departments to establish mandatory secondary review workflows for complex cases (e.g., first-time cancer diagnoses, high-grade dysplasias) prior to sign-out, as well as systematic peer-review tracking'. The guideline's published content is two strong recommendations on moderate-certainty evidence — establish formal case-review procedures to identify diagnostic disagreements and potential interpretive errors, and complete those reviews quickly enough to positively influence patient management. It does not specify mandatory pre-sign-out secondary review of the named case categories, and a resident citing that requirement would be citing something that is not there. Rewritten to the actual recommendations, with the timeliness element foregrounded because it is the substantive addition and the submission missed it entirely.

title: 2024 McDonald Criteria: Kappa Free Light Chains Accepted Interchangeably with Oligoclonal Bands
journal: Lancet Neurology and Nature Reviews Neurology (implementation)
breakthrough: The 2024 revisions of the McDonald diagnostic criteria for multiple sclerosis accept CSF kappa free light chain testing as an alternative to oligoclonal IgG bands, usable interchangeably for the CSF-positivity component. Diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of κ-FLC are equivalent to oligoclonal bands at the 95% confidence level, with a κ-FLC index of ≥6.1 performing best. Concordance between the two is around 90%, so in rare discordant cases determining both remains appropriate.
impact: Replaces a manual, rater-dependent isoelectric focusing gel read with an automated quantitative immunoassay of equal diagnostic performance — a genuine improvement in reproducibility and turnaround for a test that gates an MS diagnosis.
practical: A laboratory can offer κ-FLC index on an automated platform with faster turnaround and no interpreter variability, and report a numeric index against a ≥6.1 cut-off rather than a subjective band count. Two points of precision matter: the criteria treat κ-FLC as INTERCHANGEABLE with oligoclonal bands, not as a replacement that retires them, and with roughly 90% concordance the two are not identical, so keep oligoclonal band capability available for the discordant or borderline case.
link: Nature Reviews Neurology — implementation of the 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria

verify.status: corrected — year of the criteria, and 'replace' is too strong
verify.note: Real and correctly identified in substance: the McDonald revisions do accept CSF kappa free light chain testing alongside oligoclonal bands, with equivalent sensitivity and specificity at the 95% confidence level, a κ-FLC index cut-off of ≥6.1 performing best, and the practical advantages of an automated, cost-effective, rater-independent platform. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) These are the 2024 REVISIONS, published in 2025 and presented at ECTRIMS — not '2026 McDonald Criteria Updates' as submitted. Getting the edition right matters because clinicians look these criteria up by year. (2) The submission says κ-FLC 'formally replace' oligoclonal band detection via isoelectric focusing. The revisions make them INTERCHANGEABLE; concordance is around 90% and the sources advise determining both in rare cases. A laboratory that read 'replace' and decommissioned its isoelectric focusing capability would have acted on the wrong word, so the distinction is stated explicitly.

title: Pathology AI Is Regulated as Software-as-an-IVD, Not as Software-as-a-Medical-Device
breakthrough: FDA's framing treats a computational pathology algorithm as a component of a diagnostic assay rather than as standalone software that happens to read a medical image — the separation that holds in radiology, where the product is software and the image comes from separate equipment, does not hold in pathology. Digital pathology tools used to generate patient results, including primary diagnosis, are in vitro diagnostic medical devices. Post-market expectations under the pathology review office accordingly focus on analytical drift, assay-level adverse events and lot-traceable corrections. Through April 2026 the FDA had authorised 51 AI/ML-flagged devices in pathology-relevant review panels, of which only seven actually analyse whole-slide images.
impact: Determines what a developer must prove and what a laboratory must monitor. Treating the algorithm as part of an assay makes stains, fixatives, scanners and lab-specific protocols part of the device's validated conditions of use rather than incidental context.
practical: The practical consequence is specimen-aware validation: performance has to hold across your stains, your scanner and your fixation, and drift is monitored as an analytical property the way it would be for any assay. Keep the 51-versus-7 figure in mind as a corrective to the impression that pathology AI is broadly cleared — most authorisations in these panels are not whole-slide image analysers at all.
link: AI/ML in digital pathology and the Software-as-an-IVD paradigm: 2026 snapshot

verify.status: matched with corrections — supported, with one framing precision
verify.note: Supported. Digital pathology tools supporting generation of patient results are IVD medical devices; the pathology review office's framing treats the algorithm as a component of a diagnostic assay rather than standalone image-reading software, in explicit contrast with radiology; and post-market attention falls on analytical drift, assay-level adverse events and lot-traceable corrections. The submission's substance and its implication — specimen-aware validation across stains, scanners, fixatives and lab protocols — both hold. ONE CORRECTION of framing: this is a regulatory paradigm evident in how the office reviews these products, not a formal 2026 reclassification announcement, and the entry no longer implies a discrete rulemaking event. ADDED: through April 2026, 51 AI/ML-flagged authorisations in pathology-relevant panels of which only seven analyse whole-slide images — a reality check absent from the submission and the figure most likely to correct an inflated impression of how much cleared pathology AI exists.

title: The Pathologist as Integrator of Morphology, Molecular and Computational Data
journal: Reviews in oncology and computational pathology
breakthrough: A recurring framing in the 2026 literature places the pathologist as the central integrator of morphological, molecular and computational outputs: routine histopathology, AI-based computational pathology and molecular profiling — genomics, proteomics and spatial transcriptomics — converging into a single multimodal assessment. Spatial profiling technologies, including spatial transcriptomics, spatial proteomics and multiplexed imaging, add a spatial dimension that maps gene and protein expression onto intact tissue architecture, which is precisely the axis a pathologist already reads on an H&E slide. Integrated analyses support molecular subtype inference, prognostic stratification and prediction of therapeutic response.
impact: Defines the role rather than the technology. As molecular and computational data multiply, the scarce capability is the person who can reconcile them against what the tissue actually looks like — and spatial methods are the ones that make morphology and molecular data directly commensurable.
practical: The near-term consequence is in the multidisciplinary meeting: the integrated interpretation is the pathologist's to author, which means understanding what a spatial transcriptomic result can and cannot support. Note the status honestly — this is a framing described across reviews, not a formal published framework from any single body, and no interoperability standard has been issued on its basis. Most spatial platforms remain research-use.
link: Artificial intelligence and the evolution of pathology: scaling from digital diagnostics to multimodal precision medicine

verify.status: corrected — the concept is real, the attribution and the standards claim are not
verify.note: The concept is well supported in the 2026 literature: the pathologist as central integrator of morphologic, molecular and computational outputs, with spatial transcriptomics, spatial proteomics and multiplexed imaging adding a spatial dimension aligned with routine architectural assessment, supporting molecular subtyping, prognostic stratification and therapy-response prediction. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) ATTRIBUTION: the submission credits the Digital Pathology Association and 'informatics leadership' with having 'formalized the "Pathologist as Integrator" framework'. I could not confirm a named DPA framework; the framing appears across reviews rather than as one body's published document, and the entry says so. (2) 'Updates laboratory information system (LIS) and image management system (IMS) interoperability standards, driving synchronized reporting across pathology, radiology, and medical genetics' — no such standards update was found, and it has been removed rather than softened, because it would have a resident believing an interoperability requirement exists. Added that most spatial platforms remain research-use, which bounds the claim.

title: Biomarker Testing in Gastroesophageal Adenocarcinoma: HER2, PD-L1, MMR/MSI and Claudin 18.2
breakthrough: First-line therapy selection in metastatic gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma now depends on four markers assessed together. NCCN 2026 principles recommend assessment of HER2, PD-L1, MMR/MSI and CLDN18.2, with broader molecular profiling where appropriate. For HER2, the CAP/ASCP/ASCO guideline requires reporting in accordance with the CAP template for HER2 (ERBB2) biomarker testing of gastric and esophagogastric junction adenocarcinoma, and asks pathologists to identify invasive adenocarcinoma and mark the areas of strongest immunohistochemical intensity for subsequent in situ hybridization scoring where reflex testing is needed.
impact: Converts tissue triage into a rate-limiting step. Four biomarkers on a small endoscopic biopsy means the block has to be sectioned with the whole panel in mind, and running out of material is a treatment failure with no clinical explanation.
practical: Plan sectioning for the full panel at the outset rather than sequentially. Note the state of guidance on the newest marker: claudin 18.2 immunohistochemistry is entering routine practice as a targeted-therapy biomarker, but no specific practical testing guideline has yet been published for it — a practical-approach paper in Modern Pathology is what exists, so any scoring threshold quoted is not from a guideline. The HER2 workflow (IHC with reflex ISH, marking the strongest area for scoring) is guideline-backed.
link: CAP — HER2 testing and clinical decision making in gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma

verify.status: corrected — wrong issuing body for the newest biomarker guidance
verify.note: Partly right, with the attribution wrong where it matters most. The HER2 content checks out and is a real CAP/ASCP/ASCO guideline: reporting per the CAP HER2 (ERBB2) template, identifying invasive adenocarcinoma and marking the strongest-intensity areas for subsequent in situ hybridization, IHC with reflex ISH. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) The submission says 'Updated clinical guidelines presented at USCAP established refined testing cascades for HER2, Claudin 18.2, and MMR/MSI' and that these set 'strict tissue-sampling and scoring thresholds for emerging targeted biomarkers like Claudin 18.2'. The four-marker panel recommendation is NCCN 2026, not a CAP or USCAP guideline, and for claudin 18.2 the literature states explicitly that no specific practical testing guidelines have been proposed yet — a Modern Pathology practical-approach paper is what exists. There are therefore no guideline scoring thresholds for CLDN18.2 to cite, and the entry says so. (2) PD-L1 was missing from the submitted panel and has been added, since it is one of the four markers driving first-line choice. The tissue-triage message was the submission's strongest point and is kept.

title: Rapid Whole-Genome Sequencing for Critically Ill Infants
breakthrough: Rapid whole-genome sequencing can return actionable findings within 24 to 72 hours in the fastest programmes, reducing time to diagnosis by 77 to 90% against conventional workflows. Diagnostic yields cluster between 32 and 57% — one series reported 32% confirmed plus 7% likely diagnostic, another 43% against 10% for standard diagnostic methods, and the Kingsmore series 57%. Clinical management changed in 52% of cases in that series and in up to 87% of infants in one Level IV NICU. Real-world turnaround is more variable: a 100-infant study reported a median of 13 days, and a pilot a mean of 169 hours.
impact: Displaces stepwise single-gene testing in the critically ill neonate, where the diagnostic question has to be answered inside the window in which treatment decisions are being made rather than after them.
practical: Distinguish the achievable from the typical when arguing for a programme: 24 to 72 hours is what a mature rapid pipeline delivers, while median real-world turnaround in published cohorts is often a week or more, and the gap is logistics — consent, sample transport, analyst availability — not sequencing chemistry. The yield is high enough to justify first-line use, and roughly half of diagnoses change management, which is the number that funds the service. Variant interpretation in an acute setting needs the pathologist, geneticist and laboratory director working together in real time.
link: Pediatric Research — diagnostic yield and clinical utility of genome sequencing in critically ill infants

verify.status: matched with corrections — supported, with real-world turnaround restored
verify.note: Verified and quantified. Actionable findings in 24-72 hours in the fastest programmes with a 77-90% reduction in time to diagnosis, diagnostic yields of 32-39%, 43% (against 10% for standard methods) and 57%, and management change in 52% and up to 87% depending on setting — all confirmed and added, since the submission asserted turnaround and utility without numbers. ONE CORRECTION: the submission states that adoption 'cut molecular diagnostic turnaround times to under 24-48 hours for critically ill infants' as a general fact. Published real-world medians are considerably longer — 13 days in a 100-infant study, 169 hours in a pilot — so the entry separates what a mature pipeline achieves from what published cohorts typically report, and names the reason for the gap. A resident promising a 24-hour result on the basis of the submitted version would be promising the best case as the norm.

title: Digital Pathology Security and Retention in CAP Accreditation
journal: College of American Pathologists checklists, reported in CAP TODAY
breakthrough: The checklist section previously titled 'Telepathology and Remote Data Assessment' is now 'Digital Pathology Including Remote Data Assessment', reflecting that the technology is no longer a special case. Security procedures must be in place and followed, particularly where portable mobile devices are used in public places. Digital images used for diagnosis must be retained for 10 years where the original glass slides are not available. Laboratories using digital imaging, remote slide review or telepathology are expected to have validation studies, training documentation and quality monitoring procedures in place.
impact: Attaches concrete, inspectable obligations to digital sign-out. The retention rule in particular has an operational consequence that is easy to miss: once a diagnosis rests on an image rather than a slide, the image inherits the slide's retention duty.
practical: Two things to check now. Whether images used diagnostically without a retained glass slide are actually kept for 10 years, storage cost being the usual reason they are not. And whether the pathologist reviewing cases on a laptop in a public place has a documented security procedure covering it, since that scenario is named. Cloud platforms bring scalability and can improve security, but onboarding new vendors and instruments against stringent security requirements is the recognised friction.
link: CAP TODAY — digital path practices reflected in latest checklist changes

verify.status: corrected — one mandated standard does not exist
verify.note: Partly real. Confirmed: the 2025 checklist edition released 9 December renamed the section from 'Telepathology and Remote Data Assessment' to 'Digital Pathology Including Remote Data Assessment'; security procedures are required particularly for portable mobile devices used in public places; digital images used for diagnosis must be retained for 10 years where original glass slides are unavailable; validation, training documentation and quality monitoring are expected. Cybersecurity and image management are acknowledged concerns and LIS-IMS integration is an active discussion. ONE CORRECTION: the submission states that 'Revised CAP accreditation criteria mandated enhanced cybersecurity, encryption, and vendor-neutral archive (VNA) standards for cloud-based digital pathology platforms'. No vendor-neutral-archive requirement was found in CAP accreditation, and the encryption and data-sovereignty specifics were not confirmed either — a laboratory told it must adopt a VNA to pass inspection would be acting on something that does not exist. Replaced with the requirements that are documented, which are more actionable in any case. The submission's conclusion about seamless inter-institutional consultation is an aspiration rather than an accreditation outcome and is not asserted.

title: Automated Digital Cell Morphology in Peripheral Blood and Bone Marrow
journal: Modern Pathology, The Hematologist and multicentre validations
breakthrough: Digital morphology analysers that locate and display images of white cells, red cells and platelets from stained peripheral blood films are commercially established, and AI-assisted digital cytomorphology has extended to bone marrow aspirates. Morphogo performed automatic bone marrow cell classification with 95.4% of classified cells correctly classified, and a 2024 multicentre clinical trial of the Scopio platform showed high concordance with manual microscopy alongside greater standardisation, sensitivity and workflow efficiency. Automated pipelines can count far more cells than a human examiner feasibly could, which reduces the variance inherent in a manual differential.
impact: The gain is reproducibility before it is throughput. A manual 200-cell differential carries sampling variance that an automated count over thousands of cells removes, and that variance is invisible in the report.
practical: The limitation is where it matters most: certain neoplastic bone marrow cells are notably difficult for automated digital morphology to classify, and this can significantly affect cytomorphological diagnosis — so the abnormal marrow, the case you most want help with, is the case that still needs the hematopathologist. Validate against your own case mix, including the dysplastic and blastic cases, rather than on normal marrows.
link: The Hematologist — digital microscopy and artificial intelligence in bone marrow evaluation

verify.status: corrected — the headline figure was not verified and a key limitation was omitted
verify.note: The direction is supported: digital morphology analysers are established for peripheral blood, AI-assisted digital cytomorphology has extended to bone marrow, Morphogo reported 95.4% of classified cells correctly classified, and a 2024 multicentre trial of the Scopio platform showed high concordance with manual microscopy plus better standardisation, sensitivity and workflow efficiency. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) FIGURE NOT VERIFIED: the submission claims these systems 'reduce manual microscopic blood smear review rates by over 60%'. I could not confirm that figure and it is not asserted; the reproducibility gain from counting far more cells is substituted, which is the benefit the literature does support. (2) OMITTED LIMITATION: certain neoplastic bone marrow cells are notably challenging for automated digital morphology and this can significantly affect cytomorphological diagnosis. The submission's conclusion — that hematopathologists can 'focus exclusively on difficult or abnormal cases' — reads as though the automation is reliable on abnormal marrows, which is the opposite of the reported weakness. Added, with the recommendation to validate on dysplastic and blastic cases rather than normal marrows.

title: Clinical Decision Support for Laboratory Utilisation Management
journal: Clinical Biochemistry and the ELMO cluster randomised trial
breakthrough: Electronic health record-based decision support for laboratory ordering works through several mechanisms: rules on test frequency such as daily labs, restriction of tests by location or patient population, best practice advisories against unnecessary repeat testing, and removal of pre-checked laboratory tests from order sets. Predictive decision support embedded in the EHR has been developed specifically to target low-yield repetitive testing in hospitalised patients, and clinicians themselves identify culture and simple unawareness of existing repeat orders as the drivers of overuse. The ELMO cluster randomised trial showed that decision support improved the appropriateness of laboratory test ordering in primary care WITHOUT increasing diagnostic error.
impact: The ELMO result is the important one. The standing objection to restricting test ordering is that something will be missed, and a randomised trial found appropriateness improved with no increase in diagnostic error.
practical: The intervention with the least resistance and a real effect is removing pre-checked tests from order sets — most repeat ordering is inherited from an order set rather than chosen. Pair any programme with a dashboard tracking total volumes, tests per admission and per admission-day, cost saving and balancing measures, so that harm from under-testing would be visible. Note that published evidence is mostly quality-improvement reports plus one primary care cluster trial, not multi-year outcome studies from academic centres.
link: Targeting repetitive laboratory testing with EHR-embedded predictive decision support

verify.status: matched with corrections — supported, evidence base characterised accurately
verify.note: The direction is well supported: EHR-embedded decision support, frequency rules, best practice advisories, removal of pre-checked labs from order sets, and dashboards tracking volumes, tests per admission-day, cost savings and balancing measures. ADDED, and it is the most useful thing here: the ELMO cluster randomised trial found decision support improved appropriateness of laboratory ordering in primary care without increasing diagnostic error, which is the direct answer to the objection that stewardship causes missed diagnoses. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) The submission says 'Major academic medical centers published multi-year outcomes demonstrating' the effect; what I found is a pre-implementation study, quality-improvement programme reports and one primary care cluster randomised trial — the entry characterises the evidence accordingly rather than implying long-run academic outcome data. (2) 'Reduces diagnostic phlebotomy-induced anemia in long-stay patients' is a plausible mechanism but was not a demonstrated outcome of these interventions, and is not asserted as one.
